title: Fake Alerts, OTPs and Phishing
intro: Learn how fake alerts, OTP calls and phishing links trick people, and the quick checks that stop them before any money moves.
recap: An OTP, PIN or password is for your eyes only. Nobody who is really helping you needs it.
A text saying money has arrived is not proof. Check your balance in your own bank app.
Check the sender, the link and what they ask for, not the logo or how polished it looks.
If someone you know sends an odd money request, call them on their usual number.

aiTutor.recap: This lesson covers the scams that reach you by call, text or chat, and the one code you must never share. The thief cannot approve a transfer without your OTP, so the whole trick is to get you to give it away.
aiTutor.example: Emeka's real bank sends an OTP only when he starts a payment himself. The call came first, and the code arrived while the caller was talking. That order is the clue: a code you did not ask for means someone else is trying to act as you.
aiTutor.watchOut: The caller sounds calm and knows your name, and may even know the last digits of your account. None of that proves they work for your bank, because such details can be bought or stolen.
aiTutor.tryThis: Look at your bank's official app or card. Find the customer care number printed there and save it in your phone under a name you will recognise.

glossary.definition: One-Time Password: a short code sent to your phone to confirm it is really you. Anyone who has it can act as you, so it is never shared.
glossary.example: You send money in your bank app and get an OTP by text. You type it in yourself. If a caller asks you to read it out, they are trying to approve their own payment.

glossary.definition: Personal Identification Number: the secret number that lets you use your card or account. Only you should ever know it.
glossary.example: A real bank never calls to ask for your PIN. If you hear "please confirm your PIN", it is a scam.

paragraphs: Made-up story: Emeka's phone rings. "This is your bank's security team. Someone is trying to take money from your account. We will stop it, but we just sent you a code. Read it to me now."
The code is an OTP, a one-time password. Its only job is to prove that you are approving something. When Emeka reads it out, he is approving the thief's transfer himself.
Remember this rule: an OTP, a PIN or a password is for your eyes only. Nobody who is really helping you needs it, not a bank, not a company, not the police.

aiTutor.explain: Ask two questions: who started this call, and what does the caller want from me? A caller who starts the conversation and wants a code is the opposite of how a real bank works. Hanging up and calling back puts you in control.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not stay on the line to "verify" them. Scammers are skilled at sounding sure, and a long conversation gives them more chances to pressure you.

widgetData.question: Someone calls saying they are from your bank and asks you to read out the code just sent to your phone. What is the best move?

options.text: Read out the code quickly, because they are protecting your money.
Hang up. Then call your bank on the number on your card or in its official app.
Ask them to prove who they are, then read it out if they sound sure.

widgetData.explanation: The code approves an action, so it must never be read out. Calling back on a number you already trust lets you reach the real bank, even if the first call looked genuine.
widgetData.bonusFact: Scammers can make a call look like it comes from a trusted number, so the number on your screen proves nothing. That is why you call back yourself, on a number from your card or official app.

aiTutor.explain: Tap each part of the message. A scam message usually has all four, and finding any two is enough reason to stop and check another way.
aiTutor.example: "FIRST-BANK: Your account will be blocked in 1 hour. Confirm your PIN at bit.ly/xyz." It has a look-alike sender, a deadline, a link and a request for a secret.
aiTutor.watchOut: Short links hide where they lead. A link that looks harmless can still open a copy of your bank's login page.
aiTutor.tryThis: Open a recent bank text you trust. Notice how it names a specific transaction and asks you to do nothing urgent.

nodes.label: 1. Sender
nodes.title: The sender looks right but is not
nodes.definition: The name may match your bank, but the number or address behind it is different, or is a plain personal number or a free email address. Display names are easy to fake.
nodes.bonusFact: Faking how a sender looks is called spoofing. It is cheap and common, so judge the message by what it asks, not by who it claims to be.

nodes.label: 2. Deadline
nodes.title: A deadline to rush you
nodes.definition: "Your account will be blocked in one hour". The deadline is the urgency lever from lesson 1.
nodes.bonusFact: Real banks do not freeze your account over a text that expires in minutes. A genuine problem gives you time to check properly.

nodes.label: 3. Link
nodes.title: A link to a fake page
nodes.definition: The link leads to a copy of a real login page. Whatever you type goes straight to the scammer. A short or odd-looking address is a red flag.
nodes.bonusFact: Open your bank's own app or type its address yourself, instead of tapping a link in a message.

nodes.label: 4. The ask
nodes.title: A request for secrets
nodes.definition: Your PIN, OTP, password, card number or ID numbers such as your BVN. A real organisation can see what it needs without asking you to type or read out your secrets.
nodes.bonusFact: If a message asks for a secret, treat it as a scam until you have checked another way.

widgetData.completionMessage: You have inspected all four parts of a phishing message.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: Check the sender, the deadline, the link and the ask. Two or more warning signs is enough to stop, and one is worth a second look.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false. Think about what proves that money has really arrived, and who you can trust to confirm it.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each statement, ask: what could go wrong if I believed this without checking another way?

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: A text that says money has arrived is proof that it arrived.
cards.explanation: Fake credit alerts are used against sellers. Check your balance in your own bank app before you hand over goods.
cards.bonusFact: Wait for the balance in your own bank app, not the text, before you release goods.

cards.statement: You should never share your OTP, PIN or password with anyone who contacts you.
cards.explanation: These secrets exist so that only you can approve things. Sharing them hands your account to someone else.
cards.bonusFact: Your bank does not need your OTP from you. If someone asks for it, it is not your bank.

cards.statement: A link is safe if the message looks professional and has a logo.
cards.explanation: Logos and polished wording are easy to copy. Judge the sender, the link and the ask instead.
cards.bonusFact: Open the official app, or type the website address yourself, instead of tapping the link.

cards.statement: If someone you know sends an odd message asking for money, call them on their usual number to check.
cards.explanation: Accounts can be taken over, and numbers can be copied. A call to the real person settles it.
cards.bonusFact: Agree a family code word for money requests, so you can quickly tell the real person.

aiTutor.review: Match each situation to the safer response. Notice the pattern: in every case you stop using the channel the scammer gave you, and check through one you chose yourself.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not reply to the message to ask if it is real. A scammer will simply say yes.

widgetData.instruction: Match each situation to the safest response:

pairs.left: A text with a link says your account is blocked
pairs.right: Open your bank's own app instead

pairs.left: A caller asks you to read out a code
pairs.right: Hang up and call the bank yourself

pairs.left: A buyer shows you a credit alert text
pairs.right: Check your balance in your app

pairs.left: A friend's chat asks you urgently for money
pairs.right: Phone your friend on their usual number

widgetData.explanation: In each case you stop using the channel the scammer gave you, and check through one you chose yourself.

aiTutor.review: One rule covers the whole lesson. It has no exceptions, which makes it easy to remember and easy to teach to someone else.
aiTutor.tryThis: Tell one person who is not online much that a bank will never ask for their OTP or PIN.

widgetData.template: Your OTP, PIN and password are for your eyes only, so {blank} should ever be told them.
widgetData.explanation: Anyone who really helps you can do it without your secrets. Anyone who asks for them, however politely, is a risk.
widgetData.bonusFact: Changing your PIN or password right away limits the damage if you ever shared one by mistake. Then tell your bank what happened.
